title: Letters that open doors — the formal letter and the proposal
goal: Write an Indonesian official letter from letterhead to signature with its fixed formulas (*Dengan hormat, Sehubungan dengan, Bersama ini, Demikian, Hormat kami*), follow it up by phone in the right register, and spell compound words the way EYD wants them.
bekal: open, build and close an official letter: *Sehubungan dengan …, kami bermaksud …; Bersama ini kami lampirkan …; Demikian surat ini kami sampaikan.*
follow up a letter on the phone: *Saya ingin menindaklanjuti surat kami tanggal …*
write compounds apart or joined correctly: *tanda tangan*, *bertanda tangan*, *menandatangani*

dialogs.title: Dialogue — Surat untuk kementerian
dialogs.intro: Wednesday, 31 January 2029. The corrected profile has been accepted, and Program Jembatan now wants a formal meeting (*audiensi*) with Ibu Maria to propose a teacher exchange. Sarah and Fajar draft the cover letter for the proposal.

notes: **Yth.** is short for *Yang terhormat*, “the honoured”, and stands before the addressee's name or position: *Yth. Ibu Maria Simanjuntak*. It is always written with a full stop. Style guides recommend dropping the *Kepada* that many people still put in front of it, since *Yth.* already does the job.

**Dengan hormat,** — literally “with respect” — is the salutation, the Indonesian “Dear Sir or Madam”, and it takes a comma. Its partner at the bottom of the letter, just above the signature, is *Hormat kami,* (“our respects”), the equivalent of “Yours faithfully”.

**Sehubungan dengan** — “in connection with, with regard to” — is the classic opening of the first paragraph. Close relatives: *Menindaklanjuti …* (following up …), *Berdasarkan …* (on the basis of …), *Dalam rangka …* (in the framework of, for the purpose of …).

**Bermaksud mengajukan permohonan** — “intend to submit a request”. *Mengajukan* (to put forward, submit) and *permohonan* (a request, application, from *mohon*) are the backbone of formal requests. Formal Indonesian asks with nouns: not “can we meet?” but “we submit a request for a meeting”.

**Iye, usulin, milih — Fajar's Betawi.** *Iye* is the Betawi *iya*; *usulin* is *usulkan*; *milih* is *memilih*. *Iye, iye* said twice means “yes, all right, I get it”. Sarah's *Mantap!* (“solid, great”) is the casual Jakarta seal of approval.

**Nomor surat and perihal.** Every official letter carries a reference number such as *012/PJ/I/2029*: a serial number, the institution's code, the month in Roman numerals and the year. *Lampiran* states how many attachments there are, and *Perihal* (or *Hal*) is the subject line.

grammars.title: The fixed formulas of the official letter
body: Indonesian official letters are built from formulas, and readers expect them in this order. Getting them right is not a matter of style: it signals that you know how things are done.

head: Part
Formula
English
rows: This is the content of our letter.
*Atas perhatian dan kerja sama Bapak/Ibu, kami ucapkan terima kasih.*
Thank you for your attention and cooperation.

after: In a letter to a named official, thank *Bapak* or *Ibu*, not *-nya*: *atas perhatian Ibu*. *Terima kasih atas perhatiannya* belongs to presentations, where you thank a whole room.
The letter speaks for the institution, so it is *kami* from beginning to end, never *saya*, even though only Sarah signs it.

grammars.title: Object first: kami lampirkan, kami sampaikan
body: Letters prefer the object-first passive you met in A1 (*Sudah saya kirim*): the document comes first, the institution acts on it, and the verb loses its *me-*.
after: *Kami ucapkan terima kasih* keeps the pronoun before the verb even though *terima kasih* is the object: it is a fixed phrase, and the version with *mengucapkan* is equally correct.
⚠️ Never write *dilampirkan oleh kami*. With a pronoun as the doer, Indonesian uses *kami lampirkan*; *oleh* is for nouns and names (*ditandatangani oleh Direktur*).

dialogs.title: Second dialogue — Menindaklanjuti lewat telepon
dialogs.intro: Tuesday, 6 February. A week has passed and no answer has come. Sarah rings Ibu Maria's section at the ministry; the phone is picked up by Tiara, Ibu Maria's secretary.

lines.literal: good, Miss. if may, confirmation-the through email to address that is-listed at head letter.

lines.id: Certainly, I'll pass that on. Is there anything else I can help with?

notes: **Dengan Tiara** — “Tiara speaking”, short for *(Anda berbicara) dengan Tiara*, “you are speaking with Tiara”. Answer your own office phone the same way: *Selamat pagi, dengan Sarah.* And *Selamat pagi* also closes the call: it is a greeting for both ends.

**Menindaklanjuti** — “to follow up”, from *tindak lanjut*, “follow-up action”. It is one word here because the compound has taken a prefix and a suffix at once; bare, it is two words. The grammar box below gives the full rule.

**Didisposisikan.** A *disposisi* is the handwritten note an Indonesian official puts on an incoming letter, saying who must deal with it. Offices run on them, so *sudah didisposisikan ke Ibu* is good news: the letter is moving, and has reached the right desk.

**Dinas** — official duty. *Sedang dinas ke Medan* is “away on an official trip to Medan”; *perjalanan dinas* is a work trip and *mobil dinas* an official car. *Cuti bersama* is the collective leave the government adds around Lebaran, when half of Jakarta goes home to the villages (*mudik*).

**Surel** is short for *surat elektronik* and is the baku word for email; in offices *email* (often spelled *imel* in chats) is just as common. *Kop surat* is the letterhead, and *tercantum* means “stated, listed” in a document.

**Akan saya sampaikan** — “I'll pass it on”, the secretary's standard promise, with the object-first word order again. *Ada lagi yang bisa saya bantu?* is its call-centre partner. Sarah's *atas bantuannya* is right here: she is thanking a service, not addressing a named official in writing.

grammars.title: Compound words: apart, still apart, joined
body: EYD writes two-word compounds as two words, and keeps them apart when only a prefix or only a suffix is added. They are joined only when the compound takes a prefix and a suffix at the same time.
after: ⚠️ So *tanda tangan* (signature) but *menandatangani* (to sign), and the standard phrase for the signatory, *yang bertanda tangan di bawah ini*, keeps its two words apart. Indonesians get this wrong all the time, which is exactly why the UKBI tests it.
A small group of compounds has fused for good and is always written as one word: *bagaimana, olahraga, matahari, kacamata, saputangan, sukarela, padahal*.

blocks.text: Write the date the Indonesian way: day, month, year, with no comma and the month in words (*31 Januari 2029*). Times use a full stop and the time zone: *pukul 09.00 WIB* (Western Indonesia Time, Jakarta's zone).
Cover the Indonesian column, read the English, and rebuild each sentence from memory.

head: English
Indonesian
rows: Welcome, Sarah! Back in Jakarta at last.
*Selamat datang, Bu Sarah! Akhirnya balik ke Jakarta juga.*
Deal. So, this is your desk. I got the laptop ready on Friday.
*Deal. Nah, ini meja Ibu. Laptopnya udah saya siapin dari Jumat.*
The Ibu Maria from the ministry? I hear she's fierce.
*Ibu Maria yang dari kementerian itu? Katanya galak.*
Of course. Which parts need correcting?
*Baik, Bu. Bagian mana yang perlu diperbaiki?*
Good. One more thing: ‘di kirim’ is written as two words. The prefix ‘di-’ must be joined on.
*Bagus. Satu lagi: ‘di kirim’ ditulis terpisah. Awalan ‘di-’ harus ditulis serangkai.*
